title: Analysing decay series diagrams
study_design: Analyse decay series diagrams with reference to type of decay and stability of isotopes

glossary.def: the sequence of stages a radioisotope passes through to become more stable. The chain ends when a stable isotope forms.
a nucleus formed by the radioactive decay of another nucleus (the parent)
the sequence of stages a radioisotope passes through until it reaches a stable nucleus

engage.heading: The habitable blue planet
engage.text:
Our planet is warm. The heat generated by Earth’s radioactivity slows down the cooling rate. Geologists have used temperature measurements from more than 20 000 boreholes around the world to estimate that some 44 TW (44 trillion watts) of heat continually flows from Earth’s interior and eventually into space. Half of that heat (22 TW) comes from radioactive decay chains. The three naturally occurring actinide alpha decay chains – thorium, uranium/radium (from U-238) and actinium (from U-235) – each generates heat on its way to ending with its own specific lead isotope (Pb-208, Pb-206 and Pb-207 respectively). The uranium and thorium amounts in the Earth’s crust and mantle are estimated to be 50 000 billion and 160 000 billion tonnes respectively. According to this estimate, the uranium decay chain alone would release the equivalent energy produced by 4600 nuclear power plants each producing 1 GW of power.

The importance of the heat supplied by radioactive decay is that it means the rotating Earth has a molten iron core, which in turn creates Earth’s magnetic field, which in turn makes the planet habitable!

chunks.heading: Radioactive decay series
chunks.text:
The naturally occurring radioactive isotopes of the heaviest elements fall into chains of successive disintegrations, or decays, and all the species in one chain constitute a radioactive family, or radioactive decay series. Three of these series include most of the naturally radioactive elements of the periodic table. They are the uranium series, the actinium series and the thorium series.

Each series is characterised by a parent (first member) that has a long half-life and a series of daughter nuclides that ultimately lead to a stable end-product – that is, a nuclide on the band of stability. In all three series, the end-product is a stable isotope of lead.

NOTE: The neptunium series is a fourth series. However, since neptunium-237 has a relatively short half-life (21 million years), neptunium-237 is no longer present in the crust of Earth but the rest of its decay series is still present and continuing to decay.

chunks.heading: The decay chain of uranium-238
chunks.text:
A parent nucleus of uranium-238 decays by alpha emission to form a daughter nucleus, thorium-234. The thorium produced in turn undergoes $β^{-}$-decay and transforms into protactinium-234, which then undergoes $β^{-}$-decay to produce uranium-234. This last isotope changes slowly by alpha decay (with a half-life of 245 000 years) into thorium-230, yet another unstable nucleus and so on.

Any such decay chain is only stopped by the formation of a stable nucleus. This occurs at the 14th generation of the uranium-238 family, when lead 206 is finally produced (Figure 3D–2).

Note that the daughters of α-decay shown in Figure 3D–2 always have two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons than the parent. Therefore, uranium-238 under α-decay becomes thorium-234.

Note that the daughter thorium-234 produced has two fewer protons and four fewer nucleons than the parent uranium-238:

$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$

The daughters of β-decay have one fewer neutron and one more proton than their parent. Beta decay therefore produces daughter nuclei that move up the periodic table.

Therefore, a thorium-234 nucleus beta decays to protactinium-234 and in turn protactinium-234, which is also a β-emitter, produces uranium-234.

$^{234}_{90}\text{Th} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta$

$^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta$

It was noted earlier that α-decay and β-decay are often associated with subsequent γ-decays (Section 3B). For example, in the α-decay of U-238, two γ-rays of different energies are emitted in addition to the α-particle:

$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{0}\gamma$

No γ-decays are shown in the chart in Figure 3D–2, because they do not produce a daughter nucleus that differs from the parent nucleus. For example, an excited magnesium-24 nucleus (with the asterisk * indicating an excited nucleus) emits a γ-ray but still remains a magnesium-24 nucleus:

$^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{*} \rightarrow {}^{24}_{12}\text{Mg} + {}^{0}_{0}\gamma$

Not all naturally occurring radioisotopes are part of a decay series. For example, the potassium-40 found on Earth is a remnant of the supernova explosion that created Earth. The half-life of 1.25 billion years is so long that these radioisotopes are still decaying from when they were formed.

section_questions.question: Which one of the following correctly describes what a decay series diagram like that shown in Figure 3D–2 indicates?
options: A. the parent nuclei and daughter nuclei
B. the type of emission (α or β)
C. the half-life of the parent

section_questions.question: In the uranium-238 decay chain, uranium-238 decays via thorium-234 and protactinium-234 to uranium-234. How many α- and β-decays occur in this process?

Use Figure 3D–2 to answer the following questions.
Uranium-238 existed in the earth 4.5 billion years ago. How much uranium-238 was there then compared to now?
section_questions.answer: Twice as much uranium-238 existed in Earth 4.5 billion years ago as half of the uranium-238 has decayed.

section_questions.question:
Use Figure 3D–2 to answer the following questions.
Why are γ-decays not shown on Figure 3D–2?
section_questions.answer: γ-decays are not shown on Figure 3D–2 because they do not produce a daughter nucleus that differs from the parent nucleus.

questions.question: What is a meant by a ‘radioactive decay series’?
questions.answer: The sequence of stages a radioisotope passes through to become more stable. The chain ends when a stable isotope forms.

questions.question:
The diagram shows part of the radioactive decay chain diagram for uranium-238.
Write down the four full decay equations shown in the diagram above and for each equation identify the parent and daughter nuclei.
questions.answer:
$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$
U-238 parent, Th-234 daughter
$^{234}_{90}\text{Th} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta$
Th-234 parent, Pa-234 daughter
$^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta$
Pa-234 parent, U-234 daughter
$^{234}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{230}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$
U-238 parent, Th-234 daughter

questions.question: Why are γ-ray decays not shown on the diagram?
questions.answer: γ-ray decays are not shown on the diagram as they do not produce a daughter nucleus that differs from the parent nucleus.

questions.question:
Some excited nuclei such as magnesium-24 decay via gamma decay.
Complete the decay equation $^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{*} \rightarrow$
What does the asterisk (*) represent in the equation?
questions.answer: An asterisk (*) indicates that the nucleus is an excited nucleus

questions.question: How many nucleons are there in a gamma ray?
questions.answer: There are no nucleons in a gamma ray (it is a form of high energy electromagnetic radiation)

skills.heading: Interpreting decay chain diagrams
skills.text:
It is important to be able to interpret decay chain diagrams such as the decay chain of uranium-238 shown in Figure 3D–2.

The vertical axis shows the mass number (A) and the horizontal axis the atomic number (Z). Uranium-238 appears in the box where A = 238 and Z = 92. This is because uranium-238 is $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$.

Alpha decays are shown by red diagonal arrows running left at 45°, which end up in a box where the mass number (A) has decreased by 4 and the atomic number (Z) by 2. This makes sense as the α-particle ejected is $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$.

This means when radium-226 ($^{226}_{88}\text{Ra}$) α-decays, the new element is $^{222}_{86}\text{X}$. A quick check of the periodic table shows that element 86 is radon, which is shown in the box correctly as Rn ($^{222}_{86}\text{Rn}$).

Beta decays are shown as blue horizontal arrows to the right, which end up in a box where the mass number (A) is unchanged and the atomic number (Z) increases by 1. This also make sense as the β-particle ejected is $^{0}_{-1}\beta$. This means when lead-214 ($^{214}_{82}\text{Pb}$) β-decays, the new element is $^{214}_{83}\text{X}$. A quick check of the periodic table shows that element 83 is bismuth, which is shown in the box correctly as Bi ($^{214}_{83}\text{Bi}$).

The other important information in the decay chain diagram is the half-life, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$, of each of the elements undergoing decay, which is given variously in units of years, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds (ms) and microseconds (μs).

For example: for uranium-238, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$ = 4.5 × $10^{9}$ years and for polonium-214, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$ = 160 μs.
